triage.name: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection
triage.reason: Infant with petechiae, jaundice, microcephaly or hearing loss; diagnosed by urine or saliva CMV testing, an important congenital infection with lasting sequelae.

demographics: Occurs worldwide; most common congenital viral infection
Most infected newborns are born to mothers with no symptoms during pregnancy
Higher seroprevalence and congenital infection rates in lower-income and some minority communities
Most infected infants are asymptomatic at birth

risk_factors.text: Maternal primary CMV infection during pregnancy
Maternal seroprevalence before pregnancy (reactivation or reinfection)
Contact with young children who shed CMV (e.g., daycare workers, mothers of toddlers)

social_history: Household contact with toddlers or young children in daycare
Occupational exposure to young children (childcare, preschool teaching)
exposures: Contact with saliva or urine of young children
Sexual contact with a person shedding CMV

chief_complaints.text: The doctor said my baby's head is too small
My baby has little red spots all over
My baby's skin and eyes look yellow
My baby was born early and small

hpi.onset: Present at birth or noted in the first days to weeks of life; sensorineural hearing loss may be present at birth or develop over the first months to years
hpi.duration: Congenital; findings present from birth, with some sequelae (hearing loss, developmental delay) emerging over time
hpi.progression: Newborn findings such as jaundice, petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly improve over weeks; neurologic and hearing deficits may be static or progressive
hpi.quality: Variable: rash is petechial/purpuric, jaundice is yellow discoloration of skin and sclerae, neurologic findings are global
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; approximately 10–15% of infected newborns are symptomatic at birth and may be severely affected
hpi.timing: Present from birth; hearing loss can be present at birth or develop later in childhood

associated_symptoms.text: Low birth weight or growth restriction
Feeding difficulties and poor weight gain

pertinent_negatives: Maternal rash or flu-like illness during pregnancy
Known maternal CMV infection during pregnancy
Maternal history of genital herpes or syphilis
Maternal history of Zika virus exposure

negatives: Weight loss after the newborn period

atypical.how_it_differs: Most infected newborns (about 85–90%) are asymptomatic at birth and are identified only through newborn hearing screening or later developmental concerns; some develop hearing loss or developmental delay months to years later.
Infants born to immunocompromised mothers may have more severe or prolonged viral shedding and a higher risk of symptomatic disease, though presentation remains variable.
The condition is congenital; the pregnant person is usually asymptomatic or has a mild mononucleosis-like illness that is not recognized as CMV.

general.mild: Well-appearing, alert, feeding reasonably; growth may be at the lower percentiles
general.moderate: Mildly ill-appearing, jaundiced, small for gestational age, with petechiae on the trunk
general.severe: Ill-appearing, jaundiced and pale, with petechiae and hepatosplenomegaly; may be lethargic or irritable
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or poorly responsive, with marked jaundice, extensive petechiae/purpura, and hepatosplenomegaly

findings.finding: Petechiae, sometimes in a blueberry-muffin distribution

findings.finding: Decreased resistance to passive movement and head lag

labs.caveat: Thrombocytopenia is a hallmark of symptomatic congenital CMV and contributes to the petechial rash.
Transaminitis reflects hepatitis from disseminated infection.
Both conjugated and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia occur; jaundice may be prolonged.
Anemia is common in symptomatic infants; values are lower than the reference range for older children.
Elevated CSF protein supports central nervous system involvement.
A mononuclear pleocytosis may be present; normal CSF does not exclude CNS disease.
Mildly low or normal; marked hypoglycorrhachia is atypical and suggests another cause.

imaging.preferred_when: Initial bedside screen in a newborn with microcephaly or suspected CNS involvement
Best characterization of CNS involvement; preferred over CT when available
When MRI is unavailable or not tolerated; avoids sedation but uses radiation

initial.why: Thrombocytopenia, anemia and leukocyte changes support symptomatic congenital infection
Assesses transaminitis and hyperbilirubinemia from hepatitis
Preferred specimen for confirming congenital CMV; collect within the first 3 weeks of life
Sensitive, easy first-line screen; confirm positive results with urine testing
Bedside screen for calcifications and ventriculomegaly
initial.only_if: microcephaly, seizures or suspected CNS involvement
suspected CNS disease or abnormal head ultrasound

initial.why: Confirms sensorineural hearing loss after a failed newborn screen
initial.only_if: failed newborn hearing screen or suspected hearing loss

supporting.why: Lumbar puncture for CSF protein, glucose and cell count when CNS involvement is suspected; CMV PCR on CSF may be added

not_indicated.why: Poor sensitivity and specificity; not reliable for diagnosing congenital infection
Does not establish the infant's diagnosis and is not needed for management

decision_points: Collect urine or saliva for CMV testing within the first 3 weeks of life; after that period, a positive test cannot distinguish congenital from postnatal infection
Confirm a positive saliva PCR with urine testing because saliva can be contaminated by breast milk
Assess hearing with auditory brainstem response and follow serially because hearing loss may be present at birth or develop later
Consider antiviral therapy (valganciclovir or ganciclovir) for infants with moderate to severe symptomatic disease, especially CNS involvement

differential.name: Congenital toxoplasmosis
differential.why_considered: Classic triad of chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcifications overlaps with congenital CMV
differential.trigger: Chorioretinitis with hydrocephalus and scattered intracranial calcifications

history: Maternal exposure to cat litter, raw or undercooked meat, or gardening during pregnancy
exam: Chorioretinitis is prominent and often bilateral
Hydrocephalus with increasing head circumference rather than microcephaly
No petechial rash or blueberry muffin lesions
labs: Toxoplasma IgM or IgA in the infant
Rising Toxoplasma IgG titers over time
Toxoplasma PCR on amniotic fluid or infant blood/CSF
imaging: Diffuse scattered intracranial calcifications rather than periventricular

differential.name: Congenital rubella syndrome
differential.why_considered: Petechial rash, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, microcephaly and hearing loss overlap with congenital CMV
differential.trigger: Cataracts, congenital heart disease or a purpuric 'blueberry muffin' rash with deafness

history: Maternal rash or lymphadenopathy in the first trimester
Maternal rubella vaccination status unknown or unvaccinated
exam: Cataracts or salt-and-pepper retinopathy
Congenital heart disease, especially patent ductus arteriosus or pulmonary artery stenosis
Sensorineural hearing loss is common
labs: Rubella-specific IgM in the infant
Persistent rubella IgG beyond the expected maternal antibody decay
Rubella virus PCR or culture
imaging: Cardiac imaging showing patent ductus arteriosus or pulmonary stenosis
Radiolucent bone disease on long bone radiographs

differential.name: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection
differential.why_considered: Disseminated neonatal infection with jaundice, hepatitis, thrombocytopenia and neurologic involvement
differential.trigger: Vesicular skin lesions, maternal genital herpes, or rapidly progressive sepsis-like illness in the first weeks of life

history: Maternal history of genital herpes or active lesions at delivery
Onset typically in the first 1–2 weeks of life rather than present at birth
exam: Grouped vesicular lesions on skin, eyes or mouth
Keratoconjunctivitis
Sepsis-like appearance with lethargy and poor feeding
labs: HSV PCR on skin vesicles, blood, and CSF
Elevated liver enzymes with severe hepatitis
CSF pleocytosis with elevated protein
imaging: MRI brain showing temporal lobe or diffuse parenchymal involvement
No periventricular calcifications typical of CMV

differential.name: Congenital Zika syndrome
differential.why_considered: Microcephaly, intracranial calcifications and neurologic impairment overlap with congenital CMV

history: Maternal travel to or residence in an area with active Zika transmission during pregnancy
Maternal rash, conjunctivitis or arthralgia during pregnancy
exam: Severe microcephaly with partially collapsed skull and overlapping sutures
Arthrogryposis or clubfoot
Macular scarring or focal pigmentary retinopathy
labs: Zika virus RNA or IgM in infant serum or CSF
Negative CMV urine or saliva PCR
imaging: Cortical thinning and malformations of cortical development

differential.name: Neonatal sepsis
differential.why_considered: Ill-appearing infant with jaundice, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, lethargy and poor feeding

history: Maternal fever, chorioamnionitis or prolonged rupture of membranes
Onset after birth rather than congenital findings present at delivery
No maternal exposure to young children or known CMV risk factors
exam: Temperature instability, tachycardia, hypotension
Petechiae may be present but blueberry muffin rash is atypical
No microcephaly or chorioretinitis
labs: Positive blood culture
Elevated inflammatory markers such as CRP
Negative CMV urine or saliva PCR

differential.name: Congenital syphilis
differential.why_considered: Jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, rash, anemia and thrombocytopenia in a newborn

history: Maternal syphilis infection or inadequate prenatal treatment
Late prenatal care or no prenatal care
exam: Maculopapular or desquamating rash involving palms and soles
Snuffles (mucopurulent rhinitis)
Pseudoparalysis of an extremity from osteochondritis
labs: Positive treponemal and nontreponemal tests in infant and mother
Elevated CSF VDRL or pleocytosis
Negative CMV urine or saliva PCR
imaging: Long bone radiographs showing periostitis, osteochondritis or metaphyseal lucencies

differential.name: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia
differential.why_considered: Isolated severe thrombocytopenia with petechiae in a newborn

history: No maternal infection or exposure history
exam: Petechiae and ecchymoses without hepatosplenomegaly
No microcephaly, jaundice or chorioretinitis
labs: Severe thrombocytopenia with otherwise normal liver enzymes and bilirubin
Platelet antigen incompatibility between parents
Negative CMV urine or saliva PCR
imaging: Head ultrasound may show intracranial hemorrhage but no calcifications

severity.mild: Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic at birth: normal or near-normal exam, isolated mild jaundice or mild thrombocytopenia, normal head circumference, passes newborn hearing screen; may later develop isolated sensorineural hearing loss.
severity.moderate: Symptomatic but stable: jaundice, petechiae, hepatosplenomegaly, mild transaminitis and thrombocytopenia, with or without mild microcephaly; feeding well and no respiratory or hemodynamic compromise.
severity.severe: Symptomatic with CNS involvement: microcephaly, seizures, hypotonia, chorioretinitis, marked thrombocytopenia and hepatitis, failure to thrive; requires antiviral therapy and close monitoring.
severity.critical: Life-threatening disseminated disease: severe hepatitis with coagulopathy, profound thrombocytopenia with bleeding, encephalitis, respiratory failure or sepsis-like physiology requiring intensive care.

red_flags.finding: Seizures or lethargy in a newborn with microcephaly
red_flags.meaning: Central nervous system involvement; needs urgent neuroimaging and consideration of antiviral therapy

red_flags.finding: Extensive petechiae or purpura with bleeding
red_flags.meaning: Severe thrombocytopenia; check platelet count urgently and monitor for intracranial hemorrhage

red_flags.finding: Rapidly rising bilirubin or conjugated hyperbilirubinemia
red_flags.meaning: Hepatitis or biliary obstruction; risk of kernicterus and need for further workup

red_flags.finding: Poor feeding, failure to thrive or hypotonia
red_flags.meaning: Systemic and neurologic involvement; may require hospitalization and nutritional support
Sensorineural hearing loss, a hallmark sequela; confirm with auditory brainstem response and refer for early intervention

complications.name: Sensorineural hearing loss
clues: May be present at birth or develop over months to years

special_populations.differences: Most infected newborns are asymptomatic at birth; those with symptoms may have multisystem disease. Hearing loss can be present at birth or develop later, so serial audiologic testing is essential regardless of initial exam.

The condition is congenital; the pregnant person is usually asymptomatic or has a mild mononucleosis-like illness that is not recognized. Primary maternal infection during pregnancy carries the highest risk of transmission and severe fetal disease.
Infants born to immunocompromised mothers may have more severe or prolonged viral shedding and a higher risk of symptomatic disease; presentation remains variable.

key_questions.question: Did your baby pass the newborn hearing screen, or has anyone been concerned about hearing?
key_questions.looking_for: Failed or abnormal newborn hearing screen; sensorineural hearing loss is the most common sequela and may be present at birth or develop later

key_questions.question: When did you first notice the yellow color of the skin or eyes, and how long has it lasted?
key_questions.looking_for: Jaundice present at or shortly after birth and prolonged beyond the usual physiologic window, sometimes with a conjugated component

key_questions.question: When did the little red spots appear, and have you noticed any bruising or bleeding?
key_questions.looking_for: Petechiae present from birth in a 'blueberry muffin' distribution; bruising or bleeding suggests severe thrombocytopenia

key_questions.question: How has your baby been feeding and gaining weight?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor feeding, lethargy and failure to thrive suggesting systemic or neurologic involvement

key_questions.question: Has your baby had any seizures, unusual movements, or seemed floppy or stiff?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures, hypotonia or abnormal tone indicating central nervous system involvement

key_questions.question: Was your baby born early or smaller than expected?
key_questions.looking_for: Preterm birth, low birth weight or growth restriction

key_questions.question: During pregnancy, did you have any fever, rash, swollen glands or a flu-like illness?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal primary CMV infection is often asymptomatic, but a mild mononucleosis-like illness may have occurred and gone unrecognized

key_questions.question: Do you work with or care for young children, for example in a daycare or preschool, or do you have a toddler at home?
key_questions.looking_for: Contact with saliva or urine of young children who shed CMV, a common exposure route

key_questions.question: Have you or your baby's other parent been told you have HIV, a transplant, or another condition affecting your immune system?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal immunocompromise, which may increase risk of symptomatic congenital infection

key_questions.question: Have you had any other children with hearing loss, developmental delay or a congenital infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of congenital infection or inherited hearing loss that might suggest an alternative cause

key_questions.question: Has your baby had any eye problems, such as an abnormal red reflex, crossed eyes or trouble following objects?
key_questions.looking_for: Chorioretinitis or vision problems that may accompany congenital CMV

key_questions.question: Has your baby had any blood tests showing low platelets or liver problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Thrombocytopenia, transaminitis or hyperbilirubinemia supporting multisystem involvement

reasoning_points: Presents in a newborn or young infant with a combination of microcephaly, petechial rash, jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly and sensorineural hearing loss
Most infected newborns are asymptomatic at birth and may be identified only through newborn hearing screening or later developmental concerns
Maternal primary CMV infection during pregnancy is the strongest risk factor, though the mother is often asymptomatic and unaware of the infection
Exposure to saliva or urine of young children, such as in daycare or with a toddler at home, is a common route of maternal infection
Urine or saliva CMV PCR or culture collected within the first 3 weeks of life confirms congenital infection; after that window a positive test cannot distinguish congenital from postnatal infection
A positive saliva PCR should be confirmed with urine testing because saliva can be contaminated by breast milk
Thrombocytopenia, transaminitis and conjugated hyperbilirubinemia support symptomatic multisystem disease
Neuroimaging showing periventricular calcifications, white matter abnormalities or ventriculomegaly supports central nervous system involvement
Dilated fundoscopy may reveal chorioretinitis, and auditory brainstem response testing confirms sensorineural hearing loss

Differential includes congenital toxoplasmosis, congenital rubella syndrome, neonatal herpes simplex virus infection, congenital Zika syndrome, neonatal sepsis, congenital syphilis and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia
Antiviral therapy with valganciclovir or ganciclovir is considered for infants with moderate to severe symptomatic disease, especially with central nervous system involvement
Serial audiologic testing is essential because hearing loss may be present at birth or develop over months to years

Failed newborn hearing screen with a small head circumference
Thrombocytopenia and transaminitis in a newborn with a classic rash
Mother reports contact with a toddler or daycare children during pregnancy

Infant with isolated sensorineural hearing loss and mild developmental delay
Newborn with jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly but no rash or microcephaly
Preterm or growth-restricted infant with mild thrombocytopenia and transaminitis
hard: Infant older than 3 weeks in whom a positive CMV test cannot distinguish congenital from postnatal infection
Newborn with a sepsis-like presentation and no classic stigmata
Infant with chorioretinitis and hydrocephalus mimicking congenital toxoplasmosis
Asymptomatic infant whose only clue is a later diagnosis of hearing loss or developmental delay
Infant with petechiae and thrombocytopenia but no other findings, mimicking neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia
